frequency table|freq.tab|table(): A count of how many individuals fall in each category (or value), built in R with `table(x)`, which returns a **named vector** with the categories in alphabetical order (Black, Blue, Brown, Green, Other for the eye-colour data). It is the starting point for a pie chart or a bar chart. See [Frequency tables, pie charts, bar charts](#/math3042-u2/frequency-tables).
named vector: An R vector whose elements carry names, such as the output of `table()`. Index it by position or by name: `freq.tab[3]` and `freq.tab["Brown"]` both return `Brown 130` with the name kept, while double brackets `freq.tab[[3]]` return just `130`. See [Frequency tables, pie charts, bar charts](#/math3042-u2/frequency-tables).
pie chart|pie(): A circle cut into slices whose areas are the **relative frequencies** of the categories: `pie(freq.tab, radius=1.0, main="...")`. Best for showing what fraction of the whole each category forms; poor for comparing two categories. See [Frequency tables, pie charts, bar charts](#/math3042-u2/frequency-tables).
bar chart|bar plot|barplot(): One bar per category with height equal to the **absolute frequency**: `barplot(freq.tab, col="lightgreen", xlab, ylab, main)`. Better than a pie chart for comparing categories against each other. For integer numerical data (`barplot(table(x))`) it is not recommended: too many rectangles and missing values along the X axis. See [Frequency tables, pie charts, bar charts](#/math3042-u2/frequency-tables).
relative frequency: A class's or category's frequency divided by the total, $f/n$, i.e. the fraction (or percent) of the sample it holds; a pie chart shows relative frequencies, and the relative frequencies of a frequency distribution sum to 1. See [Histograms: the class recipe](#/math3042-u2/histograms).
absolute frequency|frequency|f: The plain count of individuals in a category or class (the height of a bar in a bar chart or of a rectangle in a histogram). Adding the frequencies of all classes gives $n$. See [Frequency tables, pie charts, bar charts](#/math3042-u2/frequency-tables).
modal category|modal colour|mode: The category with the largest frequency, i.e. the mode of categorical data: Brown (130 of 302) is the modal eye colour. For a stem-and-leaf plot the mode is the value whose leaf repeats most (170 cm in the 20-height example). See [Frequency tables, pie charts, bar charts](#/math3042-u2/frequency-tables).
stem: Everything in front of the leaf digit when a value is cut for a stem-and-leaf plot: 163 has stem 16; 2.28 (rounded from 2.283) has stem 22. Stems are listed down the left of the vertical line. See [Stem-and-leaf plots](#/math3042-u2/stem-and-leaf).
leaf: The last digit kept of a data value in a stem-and-leaf plot: 163 has leaf 3. One leaf is written per value, to the right of the line, and the leaves on each line are sorted. See [Stem-and-leaf plots](#/math3042-u2/stem-and-leaf).
stem-and-leaf plot|stem plot|stem(): A simple, old-fashioned display that cuts every value into a stem and a leaf and lists the sorted leaves beside each stem, so it is a frequency distribution that still shows every value. R: `stem(x)`; its key line ("The decimal point is 1 digit(s) to the right of the |") tells you how to read a leaf (14 | 1 is 141). See [Stem-and-leaf plots](#/math3042-u2/stem-and-leaf).
split stems: R's habit of printing each stem on two lines when one line would be too crowded: the first line holds leaves 0–4, the second leaves 5–9 (the 302 heights). `stem(x, scale=0.5)` compresses the plot so that all ten leaves share one line again. See [Stem-and-leaf plots](#/math3042-u2/stem-and-leaf).
histogram|hist(): The most common and important chart for numerical data: the range of $X$ is divided into classes of equal width, the values in each class are counted, and one rectangle per class is drawn with height equal to the frequency, no gaps. R: `hist(x, breaks=seq(lo, hi, by=w), right=FALSE)`. See [Histograms: the class recipe](#/math3042-u2/histograms).
class|classes: One of the equal-width intervals the $X$ axis is divided into for a histogram or frequency distribution; every value falls into exactly one class. See [Histograms: the class recipe](#/math3042-u2/histograms).
class width|width: The distance from one lower class limit to the next. Start from the ideal width $R/\sqrt{n}$, then round it to the data's precision and a nice number (Age: 1.38 → 2; Old Faithful: 0.212 → 0.200). See [Histograms: the class recipe](#/math3042-u2/histograms).
class limits|lower class limit|upper cla: The smallest and largest values a class can hold. Lower limits start at the minimum (rounded down) and rise by the class width; each **upper limit is the next lower limit minus one unit of precision** (18–19, 20–21; 1.600–1.799, 1.800–1.999). See [Histograms: the class recipe](#/math3042-u2/histograms).
class mark|midpoint: The midpoint of a class, $(\text{lower} + \text{upper})/2$, used as the representative value $X_i$ of every observation in the class when a grouped mean or sd is computed (Unit 1). See [Histograms: the class recipe](#/math3042-u2/histograms).
frequency distribution: The table of classes with the number of values in each (the result of step 6 of the histogram recipe); a histogram is its direct visual representation. The frequencies sum to $n$. See [Histograms: the class recipe](#/math3042-u2/histograms).
ideal class width|R/\\sqrt{n}: Step 2 of the recipe: $\dfrac{R}{\sqrt{n}} = \dfrac{\max - \min}{\sqrt{n}}$, the width that gives about $\sqrt{n}$ classes. It is then rounded to the precision of $X$ to give the actual class width. See [Histograms: the class recipe](#/math3042-u2/histograms).
√n rule|sqrt(n)|\\sqrt{n}: Use $\sqrt{n}$ as the initial number of classes ($\sqrt{302} = 17.4$, $\sqrt{272} = 16.5$). It avoids both pitfalls: far too many classes (jagged, empty classes) and far too few (no detail about the shape). See [Histograms: the class recipe](#/math3042-u2/histograms).
right = FALSE|right=FALSE: The `hist()` and `cut()` option that makes each class include its lower limit and exclude the next lower limit, $[\text{lower}, \text{next lower})$: the rectangle over 18–20 counts $18 \le X < 20$, not including 20. See [Histograms: the class recipe](#/math3042-u2/histograms).
cumulative frequency|cumul freq: The number of values in a class **and every class before it**; the last cumulative frequency equals $n$ (272 for Old Faithful; 134 eruptions are below 4.0 min). R: `cumsum(table(cut(x, breaks, right=FALSE)))`. See [Cumulative frequencies & ogives](#/math3042-u2/cumulative-ogive).
cumulative relative frequency|cumul rel: The cumulative frequency divided by $n$: the fraction of values at or below a class's upper limit (0.493 at 3.999 for Old Faithful). The last one is 1.000. It is the Y coordinate of an ogive. See [Cumulative frequencies & ogives](#/math3042-u2/cumulative-ogive).
ogive: Pronounced "oh-jive": the cumulative relative frequencies plotted against the **upper class limits** and joined by lines, with one extra point at 0 before the first class. It shows all percentiles at once: read up from an $X$ to get the fraction below it, or across from a fraction to get that percentile. R: `plot(upper.limits, c(0, cum.rel), type="b")`. See [Cumulative frequencies & ogives](#/math3042-u2/cumulative-ogive).
percentile|P_k|P_{k}: $P_k$ is the value with $k\%$ of the data below it. On an ogive, read across from $k/100$ to the curve and down: Old Faithful $P_{35} \approx 3.0$, $P_{55} \approx 4.1$, $P_{30} \approx 2.35$. In R: `quantile(~X, probs=k/100, data=df)`. See [Cumulative frequencies & ogives](#/math3042-u2/cumulative-ogive).
scatter plot|scatterplot|plot(): One point $(X, Y)$ per individual for two numerical variables: mtcars fuel efficiency (mpg) against weight (wt). A downward trend goes with a negative $r$ (`cor(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)` = −0.868). R: `plot(x, y)` or lattice's `xyplot(y ~ x, data=df)`. See [Scatter plots](#/math3042-u2/scatter-plots).
regression line|line of best fit: The straight line fitted through a scatter plot (mtcars: `mpg = -5.344*wt + 37.285`), drawn by `abline(lm(y ~ x))` or `xyplot(..., type=c("p","r"))`. Covered properly later in the course; for now it just shows the trend the points follow. See [Scatter plots](#/math3042-u2/scatter-plots).
model formula|~|Days~Sex|~Days: R's `~` notation for "explained by / grouped by": `~Days` means just the Days variable, `Days ~ Sex` means Days grouped by Sex, `Days ~ Eth + Sex` groups by both (names A.F, N.F, A.M, N.M), and `mpg ~ wt` in a plot means Y against X. See [favstats, model formulas, percentiles, Z-scores](#/math3042-u2/lab2-grouped).
favstats|favstats(): mosaic's summary function: `favstats(~Days, data=quine)` prints min, Q1, median, Q3, max, mean, sd, n, missing, and `favstats(Days ~ Lrn, data=quine)` prints one such row per group (AL mean 15.8, SL mean 17.3). Unlike `summary()` it includes the standard deviation. See [favstats, model formulas, percentiles, Z-scores](#/math3042-u2/lab2-grouped).
mosaic: The R package used in Lab 2 that adds `favstats()` and lets `mean`, `median`, `sd`, `var`, `min`, `max`, `sum`, `IQR`, `quantile`, `histogram` and `bwplot` take a model formula and `data=`, so statistics can be computed per group. See [favstats, model formulas, percentiles, Z-scores](#/math3042-u2/lab2-grouped).
quantile()|probs=|quantile(~Days, probs=: R's percentile function. With no `probs` it gives the five-number summary; `probs=0.9` gives the 90th percentile (40 days absent); `probs=c(0.1, 0.9)` or `probs=seq(0.1, 0.9, by=0.1)` several at once; `quantile(Days ~ Lrn, ...)` one row per group. Percentages are entered as decimals. See [favstats, model formulas, percentiles, Z-scores](#/math3042-u2/lab2-grouped).
percent_rank|percent_rank(): dplyr's function giving every value its **percentile ranking** as a decimal (the first quine student: 0.0897, i.e. absent more often than 9% of students); `round(100*percent_rank(x))` prints whole percents, and `subset(df, percent_rank(X) > 0.75)` keeps the rows above the 75th percentile. See [favstats, model formulas, percentiles, Z-scores](#/math3042-u2/lab2-grouped).
percentile rank|percentile ranking: The reverse of a percentile: given a value $X$, the percent of the data below it (9 for the first quine student). Like a Z-score it says how large a value is relative to the rest. See [favstats, model formulas, percentiles, Z-scores](#/math3042-u2/lab2-grouped).
scale()|scale(x): R's Z-score function: `scale(quine$Days)` subtracts the mean and divides by the sample sd for every value (first student −0.89, i.e. 0.89 sd below the mean). `sum(abs(scale(x)) > 2)` counts values beyond 2 sd (8 for Days). See [favstats, model formulas, percentiles, Z-scores](#/math3042-u2/lab2-grouped).
Z-score|Z: $Z = \dfrac{X - \bar{X}}{s}$, how many standard deviations a value is from the mean. Counting values within $\pm k$ sd tests Chebyshev (always true) against the empirical rule (only for bell-shaped data; quine Days breaks it because it is skewed, $Sk = 1.01$). See [favstats, model formulas, percentiles, Z-scores](#/math3042-u2/lab2-grouped).
prop.table|prop.table(): Turns a table of counts into fractions of the total: `prop.table(table(P25.students$Sex))` gives F 0.622, M 0.378 among the quarter of students with the fewest absences. See [favstats, model formulas, percentiles, Z-scores](#/math3042-u2/lab2-grouped).
subset()|subset(quine, ...): Keeps the rows of a data frame that satisfy a condition: `subset(quine, percent_rank(Days) > 0.75)` or `subset(quine, percent_rank(Days) < 0.25)`; logical indexing `x[is.F0.Male]` does the same for a vector. See [favstats, model formulas, percentiles, Z-scores](#/math3042-u2/lab2-grouped).
cut()|cut(x, breaks, right=FALSE): Assigns each value to its class interval given the `breaks`; `table(cut(...))` is the frequency distribution and `cumsum()` of that is the cumulative frequency distribution. See [Cumulative frequencies & ogives](#/math3042-u2/cumulative-ogive).
cumsum()|cumsum: Running total of a vector: applied to the class frequencies it produces the cumulative frequencies (12, 51, 71, ..., 272). See [Cumulative frequencies & ogives](#/math3042-u2/cumulative-ogive).
xyplot|xyplot(): lattice's scatter-plot function using a model formula: `xyplot(mpg ~ wt, data=mtcars, type=c("p","r"), pch=19, cex=1, col="lightgreen")` draws the points ("p") and the regression line ("r"). See [Scatter plots](#/math3042-u2/scatter-plots).
bwplot|bwplot(): lattice/mosaic box-and-whisker plot: `bwplot(~Days, data=quine, horizontal=TRUE)` for one box, `bwplot(Days ~ Eth, data=quine)` for side-by-side boxes per group. The dot marks the median and circles beyond the whiskers are outliers. See [favstats, model formulas, percentiles, Z-scores](#/math3042-u2/lab2-grouped).
histogram(): mosaic's version of `hist()`: `histogram(~Days, data=quine, type="count", breaks=seq(0, 85, by=5), col="#FF7256")`; `type="count"` asks for frequencies rather than densities and the colour is a hexadecimal RGB code. See [favstats, model formulas, percentiles, Z-scores](#/math3042-u2/lab2-grouped).
paste0|paste0(): Glues strings and numbers together with no separator, used to put $n$ into a title without hard-coding it: `main=paste0("Box plot of Days Absent (n = ", nrow(quine), ")")`. See [favstats, model formulas, percentiles, Z-scores](#/math3042-u2/lab2-grouped).
cbind|cbind(): Binds vectors as columns; `cbind(v)` prints a single vector vertically, one value per row, as Lab 2 asks for the F0 male percentile rankings. See [favstats, model formulas, percentiles, Z-scores](#/math3042-u2/lab2-grouped).
quine: The Lab 2 data frame from the MASS package: 146 children from Walgett, NSW, with Days absent and the factors Sex (F/M), Eth (A/N), Age (F0–F3) and Lrn (AL/SL). Days is strongly skewed right (Sk = 1.01) with 8 outliers above 49.375. See [favstats, model formulas, percentiles, Z-scores](#/math3042-u2/lab2-grouped).
